210: The interaction between variety and storage was highly significant. The highest mean, 1.491%, was recorded for Kalojira in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.832%, for Radhunipagal at 12 months. Over the twelve months the change amounted to -31.5% in Gobindabhog, -31.0% in Radhunipagal and -31.2% in Kalojira. All three landraces shifted by nearly equivalent margins, storage having affected them alike.
211: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 1.558% was recorded by Kalojira grown at Nadia and sampled as fresh paddy, and the minimum of 0.743% by Radhunipagal grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 12 months. Given the non-significance of this term, these two extreme cells cannot be interpreted as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
218: Rice contains little fat, yet that fraction exerts an influence on keeping quality disproportionate to its magnitude. The decline through storage is most probably enzymatic in origin. Lipase cleaves the triglycerides into free fatty acids, and lipoxygenase then permits those acids to react with oxygen, which is why fat acidity rises so rapidly in stored rice that it is widely employed as an index of deterioration (Genkawa et al., 2008). Kim et al. (2023) confirmed in recent work that fat acidity and sensory quality deteriorate in concert as storage temperature and duration increase. The consequences extend beyond the loss of energy value, since the low-molecular-weight carbonyl compounds formed on oxidation of rice lipid impart the stale odour of old grain and act antagonistically to whatever fragrance remains; the parallel decline of fat and aroma in this study is therefore likely to be causal rather than coincidental, as Zhou et al. (2002) also concluded. These oxidation products additionally attack protein sulphydryl groups and promote the cross-linking responsible for the loss of protein solubility, so that the changes in lipid, protein and starch during ageing constitute one connected process rather than three separate ones (Zhou et al., 2015). The varietal differences most probably follow from differences in bran thickness, the greater part of rice lipid residing in the bran and embryo.

231: The three-factor interaction was highly significant. This range is appreciably wider than that generated by any single factor in isolation. Location, landrace and storage period operated jointly, and the optimum result is obtainable only by setting all three at the appropriate level.
238: Ash represents the mineral residue of the grain. Minerals are neither generated nor lost from grain held in store, so that no genuine change with storage is to be expected, and the very small variation recorded here is most probably an artefact of expressing ash on a fresh weight basis while the moisture content of the grain fluctuated. It registered as significant only because the experimental error for this trait was exceptionally low, and it carries no nutritional meaning. The varietal differences, by contrast, are real and are most probably a matter of grain anatomy, the husk, aleurone and bran constituting the mineral-rich tissues, so that a landrace possessing proportionately more of them leaves more ash. Verma and Srivastav (2017) found comparable differences among Indian aromatic rices and reported aromatic types to be superior to non-aromatic ones on this count. The effect of growing site most probably reflects differences in soil fertility and in the supply of plant-available minerals, and Patra et al. (2024) demonstrated that ash in a West Bengal aromatic landrace responds to the nutrient source applied to the crop.

258: Phenolic compounds constitute the principal health-promoting constituents of rice and proved the least stable of all the traits determined. Two processes most probably account for the loss. Monomeric phenolics polymerise into larger condensed forms that resist extraction by the solvent and no longer react with the assay reagent, while polyphenol oxidase and peroxidase remain partly active in stored grain and convert phenolic substrates into quinones. The drift of grain colour away from green during storage is the visible expression of the same chemistry. Zhou et al. (2004) recorded a comparable loss of phenolic acids from stored brown and white rice and found it far greater at high than at low temperature, which accounts for the severity of the loss under ambient conditions in eastern India. The varietal ranking is straightforwardly a pigment effect, a landrace bearing a coloured husk and pigmented pericarp carrying a much heavier phenolic load, as Zhang et al. (2010) demonstrated for black rice bran and Shao et al. (2014) confirmed by locating these compounds in the bran, embryo and endosperm fractions. The wide differences between growing sites most probably arise because plants accumulate phenolics in response to stress imposed by intense insolation, drought or impoverished soil, so that a harsher environment frequently yields grain richer in them.
